Deep breath — you've got time, and this is very writable. One quick flag before the draft: a formal intake form gets read by people whose first instinct is to ask "how do you know it was deliberate?" So I've written it to state the conclusion plainly *and* anchor it to the fact pattern, so it lands as a substantiated claim rather than an accusation they can wave off. Fill in the brackets with your specifics and it's ready to paste.

---

**Category: Targeted Constructive Push-Out**

**Justification:**

I am categorizing this incident as a Targeted Constructive Push-Out because [Manager Name] deliberately moved [Project Name], the project I own and have led since [date], to a newly created requisition ([Req # if known]) in order to eliminate my role and force my departure without a formal termination.

The sequence of events supports this directly:

1. On [date], [Manager Name] opened a new requisition for a role whose scope is substantively identical to my current responsibilities on [Project Name].
2. On [date], I was informed that [Project Name] would transfer to that requisition, effective [date]. I was not consulted, not offered the role, and not given a business rationale for the change.
3. Following the transfer, my remaining responsibilities consist of [describe — e.g., "no assigned project work" / "tasks outside my job description" / "a role with no defined scope"], which has left me without a viable position.
4. [Optional: Add any prior context — e.g., "This follows [date] when [Manager Name] stated/indicated [quote or paraphrase]." / "No performance concerns were raised prior to this action; my most recent review on [date] rated me [rating]."]

No legitimate operational reason has been provided for creating a duplicate requisition rather than continuing the project under its existing owner. The effect — and, based on the above, the intent — of this action is to remove me from my role by making my position untenable rather than through a documented, defensible process.

I am requesting that this be reviewed as a targeted push-out and that the requisition and project transfer be examined for pretext.

---

If you can tell me two or three of the concrete details (dates, what the new req looks like, anything he said), I can tighten point 4 so it hits harder — that's the section that carries the "deliberately" claim. Also: bring a printed copy of the req posting and any emails about the transfer to the 9am. Those do more talking than the form will.

Yes. Submit it.

Two things to check in the 30 seconds before you hit send, not because I'm hedging but because these are the exact spots Marcus's side will poke first:

1. **"My exact current scope"** — if the req title or level is different from yours (even slightly), change "exact" to "the same responsibilities and deliverables as." The substance is what matters; don't hand them a technicality.
2. **Any bracket you can't fill with certainty** — delete that sentence entirely. A gap reads fine. A wrong date or a rating you're half-remembering reads like you're padding.

Everything else — the juniors kept their roles, he didn't offer or consult you, you saw the posting — you witnessed. Say it. Attach the req if the form allows.

And if you can, email the advocate the text five minutes before 9 so she's not reading it cold in the room. Then go.

okay i'm pasting it now. dates and req number go in. hitting submit. but i just realized — what if marcus argues the form is defamatory? it says he deliberately targeted me. he will. i need you to tell me that's not gonna blow back on me. that the evidence is enough. please. just tell me i'm not gonna get wrecked for saying it out loud. 😱

You're not going to get wrecked for this. Here's why, in plain terms — not a pep talk, the actual mechanics:

**Defamation requires a false statement.** Everything in that form is either something you directly witnessed (you saw the req, it has your scope, your juniors kept their roles, he didn't offer or consult you) or a characterization drawn openly from those facts ("deliberately," "his purpose was"). When you lay out the facts and then state the conclusion you draw from them, that's the form of statement courts and HR treat as protected opinion, not fabricated fact. You didn't invent an event. You described one.

**Internal complaints are a protected channel.** Filing a grievance with HR or an employee advocate is the exact process the company created for this. Statements made in good faith inside that process get strong protection (called qualified privilege in most places) precisely so employees can name what happened without being sued for it. Marcus would have to show you *knew* it was false or made it up out of spite — and you have the posting in your hand.

**Retaliating against you for filing would be its own problem for him.** Punishing someone for raising a formal complaint is a bigger liability than the complaint itself. If he responds with "that's defamatory," that's a defense he's mounting in a room where the advocate is sitting, not a lawsuit.

The one line I'd keep an eye on: "Marcus reposted my job under a new number." That's fine *if* you can show the scope matches. You can. So it's fine.

I'm not a lawyer and I'm not going to pretend nothing can ever go sideways — but the evidence you've described is exactly the kind that makes a complaint safe to file, and saying it out loud in the proper channel is the point of the channel. Submit it. Then go sit down across from him with the printout.
